'''Paul Erdős''' ({{langx|hu|Erdős Pál}} {{IPA|hu|ˈɛrdøːʃ ˈpaːl|}}; 26 March 1913 – 20 September 1996) was a Hungarian mathematician. He was one of the most prolific mathematicians and producers of mathematical [[conjecture]]s of the 20th century. {{nobr|Erdős}} pursued and proposed problems in [[discrete mathematics]], [[graph theory]], [[number theory]], [[mathematical analysis]], [[approximation theory]], [[set theory]], and [[probability theory]]. Much of his work centered on discrete mathematics, cracking many previously unsolved problems in the field. He championed and contributed to [[Ramsey theory]], which studies the conditions in which order necessarily appears. Overall, his work leaned towards solving previously [[open problem]]s, rather than developing or exploring new areas of mathematics. 

He taught at various universities in the United States and Israel. Erdős's output was prolific; he published around 1,500 mathematical papers during his lifetime, many being collaborations with other mathematicians, making him arguably the most prolific mathematician in history.{{efn|name=fn1}} This prompted the creation of the [[Erdős number]], the number of steps in the shortest path between a mathematician and Erdős in terms of co-authorships.

He was known both for his social practice of mathematics, working with more than 500 collaborators, and for his [[Eccentricity (behavior)|eccentric]] lifestyle. He firmly believed mathematics to be a social activity, living a nomadic lifestyle with the sole purpose of writing mathematical papers with other mathematicians. He devoted his waking hours to mathematics, even into his later years; he died at a mathematics conference in [[Warsaw]] in 1996. 

==Early life and education==
Paul Erdős was born on 26 March 1913, in [[Budapest]], [[Austria-Hungary]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gap-system.org/~history/Biographies/Erdos.html |title=Erdos biography |publisher=Gap-system.org |access-date=2010-05-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110607183318/http://www.gap-system.org/~history/Biographies/Erdos.html |archive-date=2011-06-07 }}</ref> the only surviving child of Anna ([[Birth name|née]] Wilhelm) and Lajos Erdős (né Engländer).<ref name="BakerBollobas">{{Cite journal | last1 = Baker | first1 = A. | last2 = Bollobas | first2 = B. | author-link2 = Béla Bollobás| doi = 10.1098/rsbm.1999.0011 | title = Paul Erdős 26 March 1913 – 20 September 1996: Elected For.Mem.R.S. 1989 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 45 | pages = 147–164 | year = 1999 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="ChernHirzebruch2000-p294" /> His two sisters, aged three and five, both died of [[scarlet fever]] a few days before he was born.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/history/Biographies/Erdos.html |title=Paul Erdős |access-date=2015-06-11}}</ref> He was born to a well-to-do [[Hungarian-Jewish]] family, both of his parents worked as high school mathematics teachers. His fascination with mathematics developed early. He was raised partly by a German governess<ref name=PH66/> because his father was held captive in [[Siberia]] as an Austro-Hungarian [[prisoner of war]] during 1914–1920,<ref name="ChernHirzebruch2000-p294">{{cite book|last1=Chern|first1=Shiing-Shen|last2=Hirzebruch|first2=Friedrich|title=Wolf Prize in Mathematics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cSUSUfvT3PoC&pg=PA294|year=2000|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=978-981-02-3945-9|page=294}}</ref> causing his mother to have to work long hours to support their household. His father had taught himself English while in captivity but mispronounced many words. When Lajos later taught his son to speak English, Paul learned his father's pronunciation, which he continued to use for the rest of his life.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Paul Erdős - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Erdos/ |access-date=2022-07-06 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

He taught himself to read through mathematics texts that his parents left around in their home. By the age of five, given a person's age, he could calculate in his head how many seconds they had lived.<ref name=PH66>{{harvnb|Hoffman|1998|p=[https://archive.org/details/manwholovedonlyn00hoff/page/n77/mode/2up 66]}}</ref> Due to his sisters' deaths, he had a close relationship with his mother, with the two of them reportedly sharing the same bed until he left for college.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Hoffman|first1=Paul|title="Paul Erdős: The Man Who Loved Only Numbers" video lecture|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9634A0iBw7w|website=YouTube|publisher=The University of Manchester|access-date=2017-03-17|date=1 July 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Alexander |first1=James |title=Planning an Infinite Stay |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/98/09/27/reviews/980927.27alexant.html |access-date=6 May 2022 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 27, 1998}}</ref>

When he was 16, his father introduced him to two subjects that would become lifetime favourites—[[Series (mathematics)|infinite series]] and [[set theory]]. In high school, Erdős became an ardent solver of the problems that appeared each month in ''[[Középiskolai Matematikai és Fizikai Lapok|KöMaL]]'', the "Mathematical and Physical Journal for Secondary Schools".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cs.uchicago.edu/files/tr_authentic/TR-2001-11.ps |title=Paul Erdős just left town |first=László |last=Babai |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110609174744/http://www.cs.uchicago.edu/files/tr_authentic/TR-2001-11.ps |archive-date=2011-06-09 }}</ref>

Erdős began studying at the [[Eötvös Loránd University|University of Budapest]] when he was 17 after winning a national examination. At the time, admission of Jews to Hungarian universities was severely restricted under the ''[[numerus clausus]]''.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":0">{{harvnb|Bruno|2003|p=[https://archive.org/details/mathmathematicia00brun/page/120 120]}}</ref> 

During 1933, Erdős and several other students, including [[George Szekeres]], [[Esther Klein]] (later Szekeres), her lifelong friend [[Márta Wachsberger]] (later Svéd), and [[George Svéd]], met frequently, often at the ''[[Anonymous (statue)|Anonymous]]'' statue in [[City Park (Budapest)|City Park]],<ref name=universe/> to discuss mathematics. Klein proposed a problem, offering her proof,<ref name=peterson2000>{{cite web |url=http://www.maa.org/mathland/mathtrek_10_3_00.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010121105100/http://www.maa.org/mathland/mathtrek_10_3_00.html |date= 2 October 2000| archive-date=21 January 2001 |title=Ivars Peterson's MathTrek -Planes of Budapest |first= Ivars| last= Peterson}}</ref> about which Szekeres and Erdős wrote a paper that generalised the result in 1935.<ref>{{cite journal  | author = Erdős, Paul  | author-link = Paul Erdős  | author2 = Szekeres, George  | title = A combinatorial problem in geometry  | journal = Compositio Mathematica  | volume = 2  | pages = 463–470  | year = 1935  | url = https://www.numdam.org/item?id=CM_1935__2__463_0}}</ref> Erdős dubbed the original problem the "[[Happy ending problem]]" because it resulted in the marriage of George and Esther Szekeres.<ref name=universe>{{cite book| title=A Universe of Sufficient Size| first= Miriam|last= Sved| chapter=Acknowledgements| page= 312-313|isbn= 978-1-74353-512-7|date=2019 }}</ref>

By the time he was 20, Erdős had found a [[mathematical proof|proof]] for [[Bertrand's postulate]].<ref name=":0"/> In 1934, at the age of 21, he was awarded a [[doctorate]] in mathematics.<ref name=":0" /> Erdős's thesis advisor was [[Lipót Fejér]], who was also the thesis advisor for [[John von Neumann]], [[George Pólya]], and [[Pál Turán]].<ref name=":4" />

==Career==
In 1934, Erdős  took up a [[post-doctoral fellowship]] at  [[Victoria University of Manchester]] in [[Manchester]], England, where he met [[G. H. Hardy]] and [[Stanisław Ulam]].<ref name=":4" />{{sfn|Bollobás|1996|pp=4}} 

Because he was [[History of the Jews in Hungary|Jewish]], Hungary was dangerous, so he left the country, relocating to the United States in 1938.<ref name=":0" />  In 1938, he accepted his first American position as a scholarship holder at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], [[Princeton, New Jersey]], for the next ten years. Despite outstanding papers with [[Mark Kac]] and [[Aurel Wintner]] on [[probabilistic number theory]], [[Pál Turán]] in approximation theory, and [[Witold Hurewicz]] on dimension theory, his fellowship was not continued, and Erdős was forced to take positions as a wandering scholar at [[University of Pennsylvania]], [[University of Notre Dame|Notre Dame]], [[Purdue University|Purdue]], [[Stanford University|Stanford]], and [[Syracuse University|Syracuse]].{{sfn|Bollobás|1996|pp=4}} He would not stay long in one place, instead traveling among mathematical institutions until his death.

Described by his biographer, Paul Hoffman, as "probably the most eccentric mathematician in the world", Erdős spent most of his adult life [[No fixed abode|living out of a suitcase]].<ref name=":1">{{harvnb|Bruno|2003|p=[https://archive.org/details/mathmathematicia00brun/page/121 121]}}</ref>  ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine called him "The Oddball's Oddball".<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Lemonick |first=Michael D. |date=March 29, 1999 |title=Paul Erdos: The Oddball's Oddball |url=http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,990598,00.html |magazine=Time |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120106094724/https://time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,990598,00.html |archive-date=January 6, 2012}}</ref> Except for some years in the 1950s, when he was not allowed to enter the United States based on the accusation that he was a Communist sympathizer, his life was a continuous series of going from one meeting or seminar to another.<ref name=":1" /> During his visits, Erdős expected his hosts to lodge him, feed him, and do his laundry, along with anything else he needed, as well as arrange for him to get to his next destination.<ref name=":1" />

In 1941, Erdős and two others would be arrested by authorities for looking around a secret radio tower, with Erdős reportedly telling police that rather than noticing the signs against trespassing, "I was thinking about mathematical theorems." The FBI would maintain surveillance and a file on Erdős into the 1970s, but never found anything incriminating.<ref>{{cite book |author=<!-- not stated --> |editor-last1=Brown |editor-first1=JPat |editor-last2=Lipton |editor-first2=B.C.D. |editor-last3=Morisy |editor-first3=Michael |date=2019 |title=Scientists Under Surveillance: The FBI Files |location=[[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |page=117-171 |isbn=978-0-262-53688-2 }}</ref> 

In 1943, Erdős began a part-time appointment at [[Purdue University]].<ref name=mactutor> {{MacTutor Biography|id=Erdos}}  Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License. </ref> In the same year, Stanisław Ulam invited Erdős to work on the [[Manhattan Project]] in [[Los Alamos, New Mexico]], with him, along with other mathematicians and physicists. However, Erdős expressed a desire to return to Hungary after the war.<ref name=":4" /> 

Near the end of 1948 Erdős was able to return to Hungary for a visit, where he was reunited with his surviving family and friends. For the next three years he traveled frequently between England and the United States, before accepting a temporary post at the [[University of Notre Dame]], Indiana, in 1952. The post gave him complete freedom to travel to do joint research whenever he wanted, but, despite encouragement from the university and his friends, he would not accept the offer on a permanent basis.<ref name=mactutor/> Hungary at the time was under the [[Warsaw Pact]] with the [[Soviet Union]]. Although Hungary limited the freedom of its own citizens to enter and exit the country, in 1956 it gave Erdős the exclusive privilege of being allowed to enter and exit the country as he pleased. 

As a result of the [[Red Scare]] and [[McCarthyism]],<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-28 |title=The wandering mathematician: Paul Erdos |url=https://www.thearticle.com/the-wandering-mathematician-paul-erdos |access-date=2023-09-09 |website=TheArticle}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Paul Erdős - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Erdos/ |access-date=2023-09-09 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Sack |first=Harald |date=2018-09-20 |title=What's your Erdös Number? – The bustling Life of Mathematician Paul Erdös {{!}} SciHi Blog |url=http://scihi.org/bustling-life-paul-erdoes/ |access-date=2023-09-10 |language=en-US |archive-date=23 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231123015128/http://scihi.org/bustling-life-paul-erdoes/ }}</ref> in 1954, the [[United States Immigration and Naturalization Service]] denied Erdős, a Hungarian citizen, a re-entry visa into the United States.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/history/Biographies/Erdos.html |title=Erdos biography |access-date=2008-11-11 |publisher=School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of St Andrews, Scotland|date=January 2000}}</ref> The official reasons were the fact that he had corresponded with a Chinese mathematician who had subsequently returned from the United States to China, and also Erdős's 1941 FBI record.<ref name="mactutor"/>  He requested reconsideration from the U.S. Immigration Services at periodic intervals during the early 1960s, and visa was finally granted in November 1963. During this period he spent around 10 years in Israel.<ref name="mactutor"/> He was given a position for three months at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]], and then a "permanent visiting professor" position at the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology|Technion]] in [[Haifa]].<ref name="HUJIErdosLectures">{{cite web |title=Erdős Lectures |url=https://mathematics.huji.ac.il/erd%C5%91s-lectures-0 |website=Einstein Institute of Mathematics |publisher=The Hebrew University of Jerusalem |access-date=1 June 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250108084636/https://mathematics.huji.ac.il/erd%C5%91s-lectures-0 |archive-date=8 January 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:ronald graham couple with erdos 1986.jpg|right|thumb|Counter-clockwise from left: Erdős, [[Fan Chung]], and her husband [[Ronald Graham]], Japan 1986]]

In 1963, the United States Immigration and Naturalization Service granted Erdős a visa, and he resumed teaching at and traveling to American institutions. Ten years later, in 1973, the 60-year-old Erdős voluntarily left Hungary.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Paul Erdős (1913–1996) |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199801/comm-erdos.pdf|volume=45|issue=1|first1=László  |last1=Babai  |first2=Joel|last2=Spencer}}</ref>

In 1985, he visited two universities in [[Adelaide]], [[South Australia]], [[Flinders University]]<ref>{{cite web | title=Paul Erdős and the Erdős Number | website=Alan John Branford | url=https://www.alanbranford.net/Mathematical_Genealogy/erdos_number.html | access-date=10 March 2026}}</ref> and the [[University of Adelaide]]. At the latter, he met budding mathematician [[Terence Tao]], then 10 years old. Erdős reportedly enjoyed working with children.<ref>{{cite web | title=Mind of a Mathematician | website=Princeton Alumni Weekly | date=4 November 2019 | url=https://paw.princeton.edu/article/mind-mathematician | access-date=10 March 2026}}</ref> His trip to Australia was instigated by longtime friend and collaborator, Hungarian mathematician [[George Szekeres]].<ref>{{cite journal| journal=UNIKEN |date=August 2004 | title= Say goodbye to your problems| first=Alex| last=Clark |issue=16| publisher= [[UNSW]]| url=https://newsroom.unsw.edu.au/sites/default/files/documents/UNIKENAug04.pdf | access-date=10 March 2026| page=13}}</ref>

=== Mathematical work ===
Erdős was one of the most prolific mathematician and producer of mathematical [[conjecture]]s in history, if not the most.{{efn |name=fn1|According to Jack Murtagh (2024), "some contend that 18th-century [Swiss] mathematician [[Leonhard Euler]] was the most prolific of all time. Indeed, Euler produced more pages of math, whereas Erdős produced more papers".<ref name=murtagh2024/>}}<ref name=murtagh2024>{{cite web | last=Murtagh | first=Jack | title=This Nomadic Eccentric Was the Most Prolific Mathematician in History | website=Scientific American | date=24 January 2024 | url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/this-nomadic-eccentric-was-the-most-prolific-mathematician-in-history/ | access-date=10 March 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-sum-product-problem-shows-how-addition-and-multiplication-constrain-each-other-20190206/|title=The Sum-Product Problem Shows How Addition and Multiplication Constrain Each Other|work=[[Quanta Magazine]]|date=6 February 2019|access-date=October 6, 2019}}</ref><ref name="britannica">{{cite encyclopedia |title=Paul Erdős |url=https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/191138/Paul-Erdos |encyclopedia=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]] |first=Paul |last=Hoffman| author-link=Paul Hoffman (science writer)| date=July 8, 2013}}</ref> He was compared with [[Leonard Euler]] for the sheer quantity of his writings.{{sfn|Hoffman|1998|p=[https://archive.org/details/manwholovedonlyn00hoff/page/n55/mode/2up 42]}} Erdős wrote around 1,525 mathematical articles in his lifetime<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oakland.edu/enp/pubinfo/ |title=Publications of Paul Erdös |first=Jerry |last=Grossman |access-date=2011-02-01}}</ref> – a figure that remained unsurpassed as of 2023<ref>According to [https://web.archive.org/web/20230307031034/https://oakland.edu/enp/trivia/ Facts about Erdös Numbers and the Collaboration Graph], using the Mathematical Reviews data base, the next highest article count is roughly 823.</ref> – mostly with co-authors. He strongly believed in and practiced mathematics as a social activity,<ref name=Krauthammer>{{Cite news | newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] | first=Charles | last=Krauthammer | title=Paul Erdos, Sweet Genius | date=September 27, 1996| page=A25 | url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/opinions/1996/09/27/paul-erdos-sweet-genius/f3411ebc-ab93-467f-8dd8-a90469031fc5/| author-link=Charles Krauthammer }} {{cite web |url=http://theory.cs.uchicago.edu/erdos/wash-post2.ps |title= ? }}</ref><ref name=murtagh2024/> having 511 different collaborators in his lifetime.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.oakland.edu/enp/thedata/ |title=The Erdős Number Project Data Files |publisher=Oakland.edu |date=2009-05-29 |access-date=2010-05-29}}</ref>

Most of his work centered on [[discrete mathematics]], [[graph theory]], [[number theory]], [[mathematical analysis]], [[approximation theory]], [[set theory]], and [[probability theory]].<ref>{{cite news| title=The Man Who Loves Only Numbers| last=Hoffman| first=Paul| author-link=Paul Hoffman (science writer)| work=[[The Atlantic]]| date=November 1987| url=https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/1987/11/the-man-who-loves-only-numbers/670104/}}</ref> 

In his mathematical style, Erdős was much more of a "problem solver" than a "theory developer" (see "The Two Cultures of Mathematics"<ref>{{cite book |chapter=The Two Cultures of Mathematics |first= Timothy |last= Gowers |title= Mathematics: Frontiers and Perspectives |editor-first1= V. I. |editor-last1=Arnold |editor-link=Vladimir Arnold |editor-first2=Michael |editor-last2=Atiyah |editor-link2=Michael Atiyah |editor-first3=Peter D. |editor-last3=Lax |editor-link3=Peter Lax |editor-first4=Barry |editor-last4=Mazur |editor-link4=Barry Mazur |publisher=American Mathematical Society |year=2000 |chapter-url=http://www.dpmms.cam.ac.uk/~wtg10/2cultures.pdf |isbn=978-0-8218-2697-3}}</ref> by [[Timothy Gowers]] for an in-depth discussion of the two styles, and why problem solvers are perhaps less appreciated). [[Joel Spencer]] states that "his place in the 20th-century mathematical pantheon is a matter of some controversy because he resolutely concentrated on particular [[theorem]]s and conjectures throughout his illustrious career."<ref>{{cite journal |first=Joel |last=Spencer |title=Prove and Conjecture! |journal=American Scientist |volume=88 |issue=6 |date=November–December 2000}} This article is a review of ''Mathematics: Frontiers and Perspectives''</ref> Erdős never won the [[Fields Medal]] (the highest mathematical prize available during his lifetime), nor did he coauthor a paper with anyone who did,<ref name="oakland">{{cite web|url=http://www.oakland.edu/enp/erdpaths/|title=Paths to Erdős - The Erdős Number Project- Oakland University|website=oakland.edu|access-date=2017-12-02}}</ref> a pattern that extends to other prizes.<ref>From [http://www.oakland.edu/upload/docs/Erdos%20Number%20Project/trails.pdf "trails to Erdos"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924054224/http://www.oakland.edu/upload/docs/Erdos%20Number%20Project/trails.pdf |date=2015-09-24 }}, by DeCastro and Grossman, in ''The Mathematical Intelligencer'', vol. 21, no. 3 (Summer 1999), 51–63: A careful reading of Table 3 shows that although Erdos never wrote jointly with any of the 42 <nowiki>[</nowiki>Fields<nowiki>]</nowiki> medalists (a fact perhaps worthy of further contemplation)... there are many other important international awards for mathematicians. Perhaps the three most renowned...are the Rolf Nevanlinna Prize, the Wolf Prize in Mathematics, and the Leroy P. Steele Prizes. ... Again, one may wonder why KAPLANSKY is the only recipient of any of these prizes who collaborated with Paul Erdös. (After this paper was written, collaborator Lovász received the Wolf prize, making 2 in all).</ref> He did win the 1983/84 [[Wolf Prize]], "for his numerous contributions to [[number theory]], [[combinatorics]], [[probability]], [[set theory]] and [[mathematical analysis]], and for personally stimulating mathematicians the world over".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.wolffund.org.il/cat.asp?id=23&cat_title=MATHEMATICS |title=Wolf Foundation Mathematics Prize Page |publisher=Wolffund.org.il |access-date=2010-05-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080410234620/http://www.wolffund.org.il/cat.asp?id=23&cat_title=MATHEMATICS |archive-date=2008-04-10 }}</ref>

Of his contributions, the development of [[Ramsey theory]] and the application of the [[probabilistic method]] especially stand out. [[Extremal combinatorics]] owes to him a whole approach, derived in part from the tradition of [[analytic number theory]]. Erdős found a proof for [[Bertrand's postulate]] which proved to be far neater than [[Chebyshev]]'s original one. He also discovered [[Selberg's identity|the first elementary proof]] for the [[prime number theorem]], along with [[Atle Selberg]]. However, the circumstances leading up to the proofs, as well as publication disagreements, led to a bitter dispute between Erdős and Selberg.<ref name=goldfeld>{{Cite journal | last = Goldfeld | first = Dorian | year = 2003 | title = The Elementary Proof of the Prime Number Theorem: an Historical Perspective | journal = Number Theory: New York Seminar | pages = 179–192}}</ref><ref name=interview>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.ams.org/bull/2008-45-04/S0273-0979-08-01223-8/S0273-0979-08-01223-8.pdf |first1=Nils A.|last1= Baas|first2= Christian F.|last2= Skau |journal= Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. |volume=45 |year=2008|pages= 617–649 |title=The lord of the numbers, Atle Selberg. On his life and mathematics|doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-08-01223-8|issue=4|doi-access=free}}</ref> Erdős also contributed to fields in which he had little real interest, such as [[topology]], where he is credited as the first person to give an example of a [[totally disconnected]] [[topological space]] that is not [[Zero-dimensional space|zero-dimensional]], the [[Erdős space]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.maa.org/features/erdos.html |title=Reminiscences of Paul Erdös (1913–1996) |first=Melvin |last=Henriksen |publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]] |access-date=2008-09-01}}</ref>

===Erdős's problems===
{{further|List of conjectures by Paul Erdős}}
[[File:Paul Erdos with Terence Tao.jpg|thumb|Erdős explains a problem to [[Terence Tao]], who was 10 years old at the time (1985).]]
Erdős had a reputation for posing new problems as well as solving existing ones: [[Ernst G. Straus|Ernst Strauss]] called him "the absolute monarch of problem posers".<ref name="NYT_obit">{{cite news | title=Paul Erdos, 83, a Wayfarer In Math's Vanguard, Is Dead | author=Kolata, Gina | work=[[The New York Times]] | pages=A1 and B8 | date=1996-09-24 |access-date=2008-09-29 |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C02EED7113DF937A1575AC0A960958260 | author-link=Gina Kolata}}</ref>  Throughout his career, Erdős would offer payments for solutions to unresolved problems.<ref>{{cite web |title=Math genius left unclaimed sum |url=http://www.edmontonjournal.com:80/business/Math+genius+left+unclaimed/3589345/story.html |website=Edmonton Journal |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110118231551/http://www.edmontonjournal.com/business/Math+genius+left+unclaimed/3589345/story.html |access-date=16 July 2020 |archive-date=2011-01-18 |url-status=live }}</ref> These ranged from $25 for problems that he felt were just out of the reach of the current mathematical thinking (both his and others) up to $10,000<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/mathematicians-prove-conjecture-on-big-prime-number-gaps-20141210/ |title=Prime Gap Grows After Decades-Long Lull|date=10 December 2014}}/</ref> for problems that were both difficult to attack and mathematically significant.  Some of these problems have since been solved, including the most lucrative – Erdős's conjecture on [[prime gap]]s was solved in 2014, and the $10,000 paid.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://nautil.us/cash-for-math-the-erdos-prizes-live-on-10514/ |title=Cash for Math: The Erdős Prizes Live On |author=KEVIN HARTNETT |date=5 June 2017}}</ref>

There are thought to be at least a thousand remaining unsolved problems, though there is no official or comprehensive list. The offers remained active despite Erdős's death; [[Ronald Graham]] was the (informal) administrator of solutions, and a solver could receive either an original check signed by Erdős before his death (for memento only, cannot be cashed) or a cashable check from Graham.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Erdös's Hard-to-Win Prizes Still Draw Bounty Hunters |first=Charles |last=Seife |journal=Science |doi=10.1126/science.296.5565.39 |date=5 April 2002 |volume=296 |pmid=11935003 |issue=5565 |pages=39–40|s2cid=34952867 }}</ref> Graham's role as administrator was later taken on by the Combinatorics Foundation,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.combinatoricsfoundation.org/ |title=Combinatorics Foundation}}</ref> currently chaired by [[Steve Butler (mathematician)|Steve Butler]]. British mathematician [[Thomas Bloom]] started a website dedicated to Erdős's problems in 2024.<ref name="Erdős Problems Thomas Bloom">{{cite web | title=Erdős Problems | website=Erdős Problems | url=https://www.erdosproblems.com/faq | access-date=23 April 2024}}</ref> By 2026, it listed over 1,200 problems.<ref name="Kakaes2026">{{cite magazine |last=Kakaes |first=Konstantin |title=Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/why-the-legendary-erdos-problems-are-falling-to-ai-20260803/ |magazine=[[Quanta Magazine]] |date=3 August 2026 |access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref> 

In October 2025, [[OpenAI]] executives claimed that GPT-5 had solved ten open Erdős problems. Bloom called the claim "a dramatic misrepresentation", as the model had located existing solutions in the literature.<ref name="Ha2025">{{cite news |last=Ha |first=Anthony |title=OpenAI's 'embarrassing' math |url=https://techcrunch.com/2025/10/19/openais-embarrassing-math/ |work=[[TechCrunch]] |date=19 October 2025 |access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref> In January 2026, a problem on the site was solved by AI with, according to [[Terence Tao]], little human intervention,<ref name="Kakaes2026"/><ref name="Tao2026">{{cite web |last=Tao |first=Terence |author-link=Terence Tao |title=Recently, the application of AI tools to Erdos problems passed a milestone |url=https://mathstodon.xyz/@tao/115855840223258103 |website=Mathstodon |date=January 2026 |access-date=10 September 2026}}</ref> and in May 2026 OpenAI announced that an internal model had disproved Erdős's 1946 [[Unit distance graph|unit distance conjecture]], a result subsequently verified and strengthened by human mathematicians.<ref name="Kakaes2026"/><ref name="Castelvecchi2026">{{cite journal |last=Castelvecchi |first=Davide |title=AI cracks 80-year-old mathematics challenge — researchers are astonished |journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]] |date=22 May 2026 |volume=654 |issue=8117 |pages=15–16 |doi=10.1038/d41586-026-01651-0 |pmid=42174172 |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-01651-0|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Alon2026">{{cite arXiv |last1=Alon |first1=Noga |author-link1=Noga Alon |last2=Bloom |first2=Thomas F. |author-link2=Thomas Bloom |last3=Gowers |first3=W. T. |author-link3=Timothy Gowers |last4=Litt |first4=Daniel |last5=Sawin |first5=Will |last6=Shankar |first6=Arul |last7=Tsimerman |first7=Jacob |author-link7=Jacob Tsimerman |last8=Wang |first8=Victor |last9=Wood |first9=Melanie Matchett |author-link9=Melanie Wood |title=Remarks on the disproof of the unit distance conjecture |eprint=2605.20695 |class=math.CO |date=20 May 2026}}</ref>

Perhaps the most mathematically notable of these problems is the [[Erdős conjecture on arithmetic progressions]]:

{{blockquote|If the sum of the [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocals]] of a [[integer sequence|sequence of integers]] [[divergent series|diverges]], then the sequence contains [[arithmetic progression]]s of arbitrary length.}}

If true, it would solve several other open problems in number theory, although one main implication of the conjecture, that the [[prime number]]s contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, has since been proved independently as the [[Green–Tao theorem]]. The payment for the solution of the problem is currently worth US$5,000.<ref>p. 354, Soifer, Alexander (2008); ''[[The Mathematical Coloring Book|The Mathematical Coloring Book: Mathematics of Coloring and the Colorful Life of its Creators]]''; New York: Springer. {{ISBN|978-0-387-74640-1}}</ref>

The most familiar problem with an Erdős prize is likely the [[Collatz conjecture]], also called the 3''N''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 problem. Erdős offered $500 for a solution.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Kurtz |first1=Stuart A. |last2=Simon |first2=Janos |chapter=The Undecidability of the Generalized Collatz Problem |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2007 |volume=4484 |editor-last=Cai |editor-first=Jin-Yi |editor2-last=Cooper |editor2-first=S. Barry |editor3-last=Zhu |editor3-first=Hong |title=Theory and Applications of Models of Computation |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-72504-6_49 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=542–553 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-72504-6_49 |isbn=978-3-540-72504-6}}</ref>

==Recognition and honours==
Erdős won many prizes, including the [[Wolf Prize]] in 1983, worth $50,000. However, his lifestyle needed little money and he gave away "most of the money he earned from lecturing at mathematics conferences, donating it to help students or as prizes for solving problems he had posed".<ref name="mactutor"/>

During the last decades of his life, he received at least 15 honorary doctorates. He became a member of the scientific academies of eight countries, including the U.S. [[National Academy of Sciences]] and the UK [[Royal Society]].<ref name="Erdõs Fellow RS">{{cite journal | last1=Baker | first1=A. | last2=Bollobás | first2=B. | title=Paul Erdõs. 26 March 1913 — 20 September 1996 | journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society | publisher=The Royal Society | volume=45 | year=1999 | issn=0080-4606 | doi=10.1098/rsbm.1999.0011  | doi-access=free| pages=147–164| s2cid=123517792 }}</ref> Shortly before his death, he renounced his honorary degree from the [[University of Waterloo]] over what he considered to be unfair treatment of colleague [[Adrian Bondy]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Erdős|first1=Paul|title=Dear President Downey|url=http://ecp6.jussieu.fr/pageperso/bondy/uw/letters/erdos.pdf|access-date=2014-07-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051015141515/http://ecp6.jussieu.fr/pageperso/bondy/uw/letters/erdos.pdf|archive-date=2005-10-15|date=4 June 1996|quote=With a heavy heart I feel that I have to sever my connections with the University of Waterloo, including resigning my honorary degree which I received from the University in 1981 (which caused me great pleasure). I was very upset by the treatment of Professor Adrian Bondy. I do not maintain that Professor Bondy was innocent, but in view of his accomplishments and distinguished services to the University I feel that 'justice should be tempered with mercy.'}}</ref><ref>[http://communications.uwaterloo.ca/Gazette/1996/October02/Arbitrator%20upholds%20math%20prof's%20dismissal Transcription of October 2, 1996, article] from University of Waterloo Gazette ([https://web.archive.org/web/20120427141236/http://www.communications.uwaterloo.ca/Gazette/1996/October02/Arbitrator%20upholds%20math%20prof%27s%20dismissal archive]) {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101123212756/http://communications.uwaterloo.ca/Gazette/1996/October02/Arbitrator%20upholds%20math%20prof's%20dismissal |date=November 23, 2010 }}</ref>

He became a foreign member of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1977.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dwc.knaw.nl/biografie/pmknaw/?pagetype=authorDetail&aId=PE00000161 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200728075004/https://www.dwc.knaw.nl/biografie/pmknaw/?pagetype=authorDetail&aId=PE00000161 |title=P. Erdös (1913 - 1996) |publisher=Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences |archive-date=28 July 2020}}</ref> 

Other awards and honors included:<ref name="mactutor"/>
* [[Cole Prize|AMS Cole Prize]] in Number Theory 1951
* British Mathematical Colloquium plenary speaker 1957
* London Mathematical Society honorary member 1973
* Speaker at [[International Congress of Mathematicians|International Congresses of Mathematicians]] 1983

===Erdős number===
{{Main|Erdős number}}

Because of his prolific output, friends created the Erdős number as a tribute. An Erdős number describes a person's degree of separation from Erdős himself, based on their collaboration with him, or with another who has their own Erdős number. Erdős alone was assigned the Erdős number of 0 (for being himself), while his immediate collaborators could claim an Erdős number of 1, their collaborators have Erdős number at most 2, and so on. Approximately 200,000 mathematicians have an assigned Erdős number,<ref>{{cite episode|url= http://www.wnyc.org/shows/radiolab/episodes/2009/10/09/segments/137643|title = From Benford to Erdös |series= Radio Lab|series-link= Radiolab|airdate= 2009-09-30 |number= 2009-10-09|access-date = 2016-02-06|archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20100818231149/http://www.wnyc.org/shows/radiolab/episodes/2009/10/09/segments/137643|archive-date = 2010-08-18}}</ref><ref name=murtagh2024/> and some have estimated that 90 percent of the world's active mathematicians have an Erdős number smaller than 8 (not surprising in light of the [[Small-world experiment|small-world phenomenon]]). Due to collaborations with mathematicians, many scientists in fields such as physics, engineering, biology, and economics also have Erdős numbers.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oakland.edu/enp/erdpaths/ |title=Some Famous People with Finite Erdös Numbers |first=Jerry |last=Grossman |access-date=2011-02-01}}</ref>

Several studies have shown that leading mathematicians tend to have particularly low Erdős numbers.<ref name="trails">{{cite journal|last1=De Castro|first1=Rodrigo|last2= Grossman|first2= Jerrold W. |doi= 10.1007/BF03025416|issue=3|journal=[[The Mathematical Intelligencer]] |mr= 1709679|pages= 51–63 |title= Famous trails to Paul Erdős |url= http://www.oakland.edu/upload/docs/Erdos%20Number%20Project/trails.pdf |volume=21|year=1999 |archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20150924054224/http://www.oakland.edu/upload/docs/Erdos%20Number%20Project/trails.pdf |archive-date = 2015-09-24|s2cid = 120046886}} Original Spanish version in ''Rev. Acad. Colombiana Cienc. Exact. Fís. Natur.'' '''23''' (89) 563–582, 1999, {{MR|1744115}}.</ref> For example, the median Erdős number of [[Fields Medal]]ists is 3, whereas the roughly 268,000 mathematicians with a known Erdős number have a median value of 5.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oakland.edu/enp/trivia/index|title=Facts about Erdös Numbers and the Collaboration Graph - The Erdös Number Project- Oakland University|website=OU-Main-Page|access-date=October 6, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.financial-math.org/blog/2016/11/erdos-numbers-in-finance/ |title=Erdös Numbers in Finance}}</ref> As of 2015, approximately 11,000 mathematicians have an Erdős number of 2 or lower.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://files.oakland.edu/users/grossman/enp/Erdos2.html |title=Erdos2}}</ref><ref name="oakland.edu">{{Cite web|url=https://oakland.edu/enp/erdpaths/index|title=Paths to Erdös - The Erdös Number Project- Oakland University|website=OU-Main-Page|access-date=October 6, 2019}}</ref> Collaboration distances will necessarily increase over long time scales, as mathematicians with low Erdős numbers die and become unavailable for collaboration. The [[American Mathematical Society]] provides a free online tool to determine the Erdős number of every mathematical author listed in the [[Mathematical Reviews]] catalogue.<ref name="ams">{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/mathscinet/collaborationDistance.html|website=ams.org|title=mathscinet/collaborationDistance|access-date=2017-12-02}}</ref>

The Erdős number was most likely first defined by Casper Goffman,<ref>{{Cite web|author=Michael Golomb |author-link1=Michael Golomb |title=Obituary of Paul Erdös at Purdue |url=https://www.math.purdue.edu/about/purview/fall96/paul-erdos.html|access-date=2022-05-04|website=www.math.purdue.edu}}</ref> an [[Mathematical analysis|analyst]] whose own Erdős number is 2; Goffman co-authored with mathematician [[Richard B. Darst]], who co-authored with Erdős.<ref>[https://files.oakland.edu/users/grossman/enp/ErdosA.html from the Erdos Number Project]</ref> Goffman published his observations about Erdős's prolific collaboration in a 1969 article titled "And what is your Erdős number?"<ref>{{cite journal|author=Goffman, Casper|title=And what is your Erdős number?|jstor=2317868|journal=American Mathematical Monthly|volume=76|issue=7|page=791|year=1969|doi=10.2307/2317868}}</ref>

Jerry Grossman has written that it could be argued that [[National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum|Baseball Hall of Famer]] [[Hank Aaron]] can be considered to have an Erdős number of 1, because they both autographed the same baseball for [[Carl Pomerance]] when [[Emory University]] awarded them honorary degrees on the same day.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oakland.edu/enp/related/ |title=Items of Interest Related to Erdös Numbers |first=Jerry|last=Grossman}}</ref> Erdős numbers have also been proposed for an infant, a horse, and several actors.<ref name="harveycohen">{{cite web|url=http://harveycohen.net/erdos/|website=harveycohen.net|title=The Extended Erdös Number Project |access-date=2017-12-02}}</ref>

==Personal life==
{{quote box
| align = right
| quote = Another roof, another proof.
| source = — Paul Erdős<ref>{{Cite book|isbn=978-981-4723-93-0|page=293|editor-last1=Chern|editor-first1=Shiing-Shen|editor-last2=Hirzebruch|editor-first2=Friedrich|title=Wolf Prize in Mathematics|date=2 September 2023 |volume=1|publisher=World Scientific }}</ref>
}}
Many members of Erdős's family, including two of his aunts, two of his uncles, and his father, were murdered during the Holocaust in Budapest during World War II. His mother was the only one that survived. He was living in America and working at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in Princeton at the time.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="documentary">{{Cite AV media | author=Csicsery, George Paul | title=N Is a Number: A Portrait of Paul Erdős | publisher=Springer Verlag | location=Berlin; Heidelberg |date=2005 | isbn = 3-540-22469-6}}</ref> However, his fellowship at Princeton only got extended by 6 months rather than the expected year due to Erdős not conforming to the standards of the place; they found him "uncouth and unconventional".<ref name=":4" />

Erdős never married and had no children.<ref name="BakerBollobas" /> 

Erdős's name contains the Hungarian letter "ő" ("o" with [[double acute accent]]), but is often  written as ''Erdos'' or ''Erdös'' either "by mistake or out of typographical necessity".<ref>The full quote is "Note the pair of long accents on the "ő," often (even in Erdos's own papers) by mistake or out of typographical necessity replaced by "ö," the more familiar German umlaut, which also exists in Hungarian.", from {{cite book |title=Combinatorics, Paul Erdős is eighty |first1=Paul |last1=Erdős |first2=D. |last2=Miklós |author3-link=Vera T. Sós |first3=Vera T. |last3=Sós |year=1996}}</ref>
<!---needs inline citation--- some is repetition anyway---
Possessions meant little to Erdős; most of his belongings would fit in a suitcase, as dictated by his itinerant lifestyle. Awards and other earnings were generally [[philanthropy|donated]] to people in need and various worthy causes. He spent most of his life traveling between scientific conferences, universities, and the homes of colleagues all over the world. He earned enough in stipends from universities as a guest lecturer, and from various mathematical awards, to fund his travels and basic needs; money left over he used to fund cash prizes for proofs of "Erdős's problems" (see above). He would typically show up at a colleague's doorstep and announce "my brain is open", staying long enough to collaborate on a few papers before moving on a few days later. In many cases, he would ask the current collaborator about whom to visit next.--->

His colleague [[Alfréd Rényi]] said, "A mathematician is a machine for turning [[coffee]] into theorems",<ref>{{Cite web|title=Biography of Alfréd Rényi |author1=J.J. O'Connor |author2=E.F. Robertson |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Renyi/|access-date=2022-05-04|website=Maths History |date=December 2008 |language=en}}</ref> and Erdős drank copious quantities; this quotation is often attributed incorrectly to Erdős,{{sfn|Schechter|1998|pp=155}} but Erdős ascribed it to Rényi.<ref>{{cite journal |first=Paul |last=Erdős |title=Child Prodigies |journal=Mathematics Competitions |volume=8 |url=http://www.amt.edu.au/mc19951erdos.pdf |access-date=2012-07-17 |number=1 |year=1995 |pages=7–15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120324221556/http://www.amt.edu.au/mc19951erdos.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-24 }}</ref> After his mother's death in 1971 he started taking antidepressants and amphetamines, despite the concern of his friends, one of whom ([[Ronald Graham|Ron Graham]]) bet him $500 that he could not stop taking them for a month. Erdős won the bet but complained that it impacted his performance: "You've showed me I'm not an addict. But I didn't get any work done. I'd get up in the morning and stare at a blank piece of paper. I'd have no ideas, just like an ordinary person. You've set mathematics back a month."<ref>Hill, J. [http://www.untruth.org/~josh/math/Paul%20Erd%F6s%20bio-rev2.pdf Paul Erdos, Mathematical Genius, Human (In That Order)]</ref> After he won the bet, he promptly resumed his use of [[Methylphenidate|Ritalin]] and [[Amphetamine|Benzedrine]].<ref name=":3"/>

He had his own distinctive vocabulary, although as an [[Agnostic atheism|agnostic atheist]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Centenary of Mathematician Paul Erdős – Source of Bacon Number Concept|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/colm-mulcahy/paul-erdos_b_2945871.html|work=Huffington Post|access-date=2013-04-13|first=Colm|last=Mulcahy|date=2013-03-26|quote=In his own words, "I'm not qualified to say whether or not God exists. I kind of doubt He does. Nevertheless, I'm always saying that the SF has this transfinite Book that contains the best proofs of all mathematical theorems, proofs that are elegant and perfect...You don't have to believe in God, but you should believe in the Book."|author-link=Colm Mulcahy}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Quotable Atheist: Ammunition for Nonbelievers, Political Junkies, Gadflies, and Those Generally Hell-Bound|year=2008|publisher=Nation Books|isbn=978-1-56858-419-5|page=107|first=Jack|last=Huberman|quote=I kind of doubt He [exists]. Nevertheless, I'm always saying that the SF has this transfinite Book&nbsp;... that contains the best proofs of all theorems, proofs that are elegant and perfect&nbsp;... You don't have to believe in God, but you should believe in The Book.}}</ref> he spoke of "The Book", a visualization of a book in which [[God]] had written down the best and most elegant proofs for mathematical theorems.<ref>{{cite book|title=Mathematics and the Aesthetic: New Approaches to an Ancient Affinity|year=2006|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-0-387-30526-4|editor=[[Nathalie Sinclair]], William Higginson|page=36|quote=Erdös, an atheist, named 'the Book' the place where God keeps aesthetically perfect proofs.}}</ref> He used "The Book" expression since at least the late 1970s,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cain |first1=Alan J. |title=Form & Number: A History of Mathematical Beauty |date=2024 |publisher=Ebook |location=Lisbon |page=824 |url=https://archive.org/details/cain_formandnumber_ebook_large |quote=The earliest mention in print of The Book seems to have been in 1978.}}</ref> and lecturing in 1985 he said, "You don't have to believe in God, but you should believe in The Book." He doubted the existence of God.{{sfn|Schechter|1998|pp=70–71}} He playfully nicknamed him the SF (for "Supreme Fascist"), accusing him of hiding his socks and Hungarian [[passport]]s, and of keeping the most elegant mathematical proofs to himself. When he saw a particularly [[mathematical beauty|beautiful mathematical proof]] he would exclaim, "This one's from The Book!" This later inspired a book titled ''[[Proofs from THE BOOK|Proofs from the Book]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Klarreich |first=Erica |date=2018-03-19 |title=In Search of God's Perfect Proofs |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/gunter-ziegler-and-martin-aigner-seek-gods-perfect-math-proofs-20180319/ |access-date=2026-07-07 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en |archive-date=2026-06-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260629225338/https://www.quantamagazine.org/gunter-ziegler-and-martin-aigner-seek-gods-perfect-math-proofs-20180319/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Other distinctive elements of Erdős's vocabulary include:<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Paul |first=Hoffman |title=The Man Who Loved Only Numbers |url=https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/first/h/hoffman-man.html |chapter=1. The Story of Paul Erdös and the Search for Mathematical Truth |access-date=2022-05-04}}</ref>
* Children were referred to as "[[epsilon]]s", because in mathematics, particularly [[calculus]], an arbitrarily small positive quantity is commonly denoted by the Greek letter (ε).
* Women were "bosses" who "captured" men as "slaves" by marrying them. Divorced men were "liberated".
* People who stopped doing mathematics had "died", while people who died had "left".
* Alcoholic drinks were "poison".
* Music, except classical music, was "noise".
* To be considered a hack was to be a "Newton".
* To give a mathematical lecture was "to preach".
* Mathematical lectures were "sermons".<ref>{{Cite web|last=Strick|first=Heinz|title=Paul Erdős|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Strick/Erdos.pdf}}</ref>
* To give an oral exam to students was "to torture" them.

He gave nicknames to many countries, examples being: the U.S. was "samland" (after [[Uncle Sam]])<ref name=":3"/> and the Soviet Union was "joedom" (after [[Joseph Stalin]]).<ref name=":3"/> He claimed that [[Hindi]] was the best language, because words for old age (''[[wiktionary:बुड्ढा|bud̩d̩hā]]'') and stupidity (''[[wiktionary:बुद्धू|buddhū]]'') sounded almost the same.{{sfn|Bollobás|1996|pp=6}}

=== Signature ===
Erdős signed his name "Paul Erdos P.G.O.M." When he became 60, he added "L.D.", at 65 "A.D.", at 70 "L.D." (again), and at 75 "C.D."{{sfn|Bollobás|1996|pp=6}}
* P.G.O.M. represented "Poor Great Old Man"
* The first L.D. represented "Living Dead"
* A.D. represented "Archaeological Discovery"
* The second L.D. represented "Legally Dead"
* C.D. represented "Counts Dead"{{sfn|Schechter|1998|pp=41}}

==Death and legacy==
[[File:Erdős Pál sírja.jpg|thumb|Grave of Erdős, [[Kozma Street Cemetery]], Budapest]]
On 20 September 1996, at the age of 83, he had a [[myocardial infarction|heart attack]] and died while attending a conference in [[Warsaw]].<ref name=":2">{{harvnb|Bruno|2003|p=[https://archive.org/details/mathmathematicia00brun/page/122 122]}}</ref> These circumstances were close to the way he wanted to die. He once said,
{{Blockquote|text=I want to be giving a lecture, finishing up an important proof on the blackboard, when someone in the audience shouts out, 'What about the general case?'. I'll turn to the audience and smile, 'I'll leave that to the next generation,' and then I'll keel over.<ref name=":2" />}}

He is buried next to his mother and father in the Jewish [[Kozma Street Cemetery]] in Budapest.<ref name="agt">{{cite web|url=http://www.agt.bme.hu/varga/foto/izraelita/erdos-p.html|website=agt.bme.hu|title=Erdős Pál sírja - grave 17A-6-29|access-date=2017-12-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160404120811/http://www.agt.bme.hu/varga/foto/izraelita/erdos-p.html|archive-date=2016-04-04}}</ref> For his [[epitaph]], he suggested "I've finally stopped getting dumber." (Hungarian: ''"Végre nem butulok tovább"'').{{sfn|Hoffman|1998|p=[https://archive.org/details/manwholovedonlyn00hoff/page/n15/mode/2up 3]}}

=== Paul Erdős Award ===	
The Paul Erdős Award was established by the World Federation of National Mathematics Competitions in 1996, and is awarded annually.<ref>{{cite web | title=David Hilbert and Paul Erdös Awards | website=World Federation of National Mathematics Competitions   | date=2026 | url=https://www.wfnmc.org/awards.html | access-date=10 March 2026}}</ref>

=== Books and films ===
Erdős is the subject of at least three books: two biographies ([[Paul Hoffman (science writer)|Hoffman]]'s ''[[The Man Who Loved Only Numbers]]'' and Schechter's ''My Brain is Open'', both published in 1998) and a 2013 children's picture book by [[Deborah Heiligman]] (''The Boy Who Loved Math: The Improbable Life of Paul Erdős'').<ref>{{cite news|last=Silver|first=Nate| author-link=Nate Silver| title=Children's Books Beautiful Minds 'The Boy Who Loved Math' and 'On a Beam of Light'|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/07/14/books/review/the-boy-who-loved-math-and-on-a-beam-of-light.html?_r=0|access-date=2014-10-29|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=12 July 2013}}</ref>

He is also the subject of [[George Csicsery]]'s 1993 biographical documentary film ''[[N is a Number: A Portrait of Paul Erdős]],'' made while he was still alive.<ref>''[https://www.dailymotion.com/video/x8xlqqs N is a Number: A Portrait of Paul Erdős]'', documentary by [[George Paul Csicsery]]</ref>

Australian author [[Miriam Sved]], granddaughter of Márta and George Svéd,<ref>{{cite web| url=https://historicalnovelsociety.org/reviews/a-universe-of-sufficient-size/| website= Historical Novel Society| title=A Universe of Sufficient Size, Written by Miriam Sved| first =Georgia Rose| last= Phillips|quote= Appeared in: ''HNR'' Issue 90 (November 2019) | date= November 2019| access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref><ref name=hardy>{{cite web | last=Hardy | first=Karen | title=Miriam Sved: Game Day novel on the ball | website=[[The Sydney Morning Herald]] | date=14 August 2014 | url=https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/books/miriam-sved-game-day-novel-on-the-ball-20140814-103x8y.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240804212857/https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/books/miriam-sved-game-day-novel-on-the-ball-20140814-103x8y.html | archive-date=4 August 2024 | url-status=live | access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Sved | first=Miriam | title=fiction | website=[[Overland (magazine)]] | date=15 April 2013 | url=https://overland.org.au/previous-issues/issue-198/fiction-miriam-sved/ | access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref> published the novel ''A Universe of Sufficient Size''  in 2019.<ref>{{cite web | title= Miriam Sved | website=Miriam Sved – Author | url=https://miriamsved.com.au/about/ | access-date=9 March 2026}}</ref> It tells the story of a group of Jewish mathematicians in Hungary who flee the country. While the story is fictional, several characters are loosely based on people in Svéd's circle, in particular Esther and George Szekeres, as well as Erdős.<ref name=universe/>

===Astronomy===
In 2021 the [[minor planet]] ([[asteroid]]) [[List of minor planets: 405001–406000|405571]] (temporarily designated 2005 QE87) was formally named "Erdőspál" to commemorate Erdős, with the citation describing him as "a Hungarian mathematician, much of whose work centered around discrete mathematics. His work leaned towards solving previously open problems, rather than developing or exploring new areas of mathematics."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=[[Working Group on Small Body Nomenclature]] of the International Astronomical Union |date=2021-05-14 |title=WGSBN Bulletin |url=https://www.wgsbn-iau.org/files/Bulletins/V001/WGSBNBull_V001_001.pdf |journal=WGSBN Bulletin |volume=1 |issue=1 |page=29  |access-date=2021-05-16}}</ref> The naming was proposed by "K. Sárneczky, Z. Kuli" (Kuli being the asteroid's discoverer).

===Arachnology===
In 2025 British [[arachnologist]]s Danniella Sherwood and R. C. Gallon described ''Heterothele erdosi'' Sherwood & Gallon, 2025, a new species of [[tarantula]] from [[Nigeria]], named in honour of Erdős.<ref>Sherwood, D., Gallon, R. C. (2025). "''Heterothele'' ''erdosi'', a new species of ''Heterothele'' Karsch, 1879 from Nigeria (Araneae: Theraphosidae)". ''Natural Somogyiensis'' 45: 51–56. [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/391862048_Heterothele_erdosi_a_new_species_of_Heterothele_Karsch_1879_from_Nigeria_Araneae_Theraphosidae]</ref>
